newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends above 7,200 for first time, bonds unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends above 7,200 for first time, bonds unchanged.

text.p: The Dow Jones industrial average closed above 7,200 points for the first time Monday on hopes that a balanced federal budget deal would keep the Federal Reserve from raising interest rates later this month.
Bonds were barely changed, and the dollar was mixed.
The Dow Jones industrial average jumped 143.29 points, or 2 percent, to 7,214.49, beating the old mark of 7,085.16 set on March 11 and its 16th record so far this year.
It was one of the biggest point gains ever for the 30-share average, and other market averages also set records.
"It was almost like a tidal wave coming," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp. "You certainly don't try to fight this kind of a move."
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks, the NYSE composite index and the Wilshire index of NYSE, American Stock Exchange and Nasdaq issues all set new highs.
Advancing issues beat declines in the broad market, 1,963 to 674, on heavy volume of 549 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
In contrast to recent sessions, the advance swept up both large-name and small stocks.
Analysts said many of the factors that fuelled the Dow's 95-point gain Friday, which produced a record weekly gain of 332 points, were clearly still at play.

Investors were hesitant to sell into the rally due to growing expectations a capital gains tax cut will be enacted this year as part of the plan announced in Washington on Friday to balance the federal budget by the year 2002.
Investors also took heart as evidence has accumulated that inflation remained in check despite booming first-quarter economic growth, fuelling hopes the Fed may raise rates just once more.

"The market is saying it expects Fed action will be extremely limited and it's saying it doesn't care if the Fed raises rates one more time," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
Whatever the reason, computer-driven programme trading boosted the market. The result was a rally of such dizzying speed that eventually it appeared to feed on itself.
"This was a classic case of panic buying," Bleier said. "These moves are fast, furious and totally compressed, and money managers who are not fully invested are chasing this market."
Trading was so fast and furious, in tobacco stocks especially, that the NYSE and Dow Jones & Co. were still calculating the Dow index's final rise at around 6 p.m. EDT, an hour later than usual.

Tobacco stocks helped fuel the late burst, lifted by news that a Florida jury ruled in favour of R.J. Reynolds in a closely watched wrongful death suit. Reynolds' parent RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. jumped $3.125 to $32.625, erasing early losses.

The Nasdaq Composite index soared 33.91 points to 1,339.24. The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 17.32 points to 830.29, a new high. The American Stock Exchange index rose 4.08 to 572.58.
The 30-year Treasury bond was unchanged, yielding 6.88 percent.

In late New York trading, the dollar settled at 1.7325 German marks, up from 1.7293 marks Friday. The dollar rose to 1.4747 Swiss francs from 1.4710 francs, but slid to 126.54 Japanese yen from 126.62 yen.

Coffee prices rose in nervous trading after news that a fire at a warehouse in Costa Rica had destroyed stockpiled coffee. At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for May delivery closed up 3.35 cents a pound at 250.90 cents.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices topped the $9 mark for the first time since the 1988 drought in the Midwest. But a slowdown in exports kept price gains modest.
Soybeans for May delivery closed up 5-1/2 cents a bushel at $8.93 after rising to a day's high of $9.02.
Gold prices rose partly on support from news that the supposedly huge Busang gold deposit in Indonesia would not pan out. June gold at the Commodity Exchange closed at $344.30 an ounce, up $2.70.
Overseas, the London and Tokyo stock markets were closed for holidays.
